#5358. How Founders Can Reduce Platform Risk Before It Threatens Growth

One day, I woke up to a notice that our app had been removed from Apple’s App Store. For the next month or so, we racked our brains trying to find out why. We even reached out to our internal contacts, only for them to tell us that helping us could put their jobs at risk. Nothing seemed to work.

For years, the App Store’s unwritten contract seemed simple. As long as you followed the guidelines, your storefront would remain available. Then a removal notice arrives, and you wonder whether your business can survive.

In 2025, Apple removed 166,899 apps and reported just 423 restorations after appeals. As we learned, being caught in it feels like watching your business collapse, with no guarantee of recovery.

It’s not all bad news, though. We survived, and this episode taught me that platform dependency is ultimately infrastructure risk. As founders, we prepare for cloud outages and payment failures, but losing access to the platform that brings us customers deserves the same attention. Fortunately, we were prepared, and this is how you can be, too.

Financially, Apple immediately freezes funds from the previous three months and turns off recurring subscriptions. For a subscription-dependent company, this can send its monthly recurring revenue to zero.

Before spending another cent on acquisition, consider what would happen to those customers if your app disappeared tomorrow. Could they still use your product and continue paying you?

If the answer is no, every new customer makes your business more dependent on a platform decision you cannot control.

Cal AI, reportedly generating $100,000 daily, was pulled without warning and later reappeared. But its reinstatement tells you little about how long your business might wait.

In Intch’s case, the explanation was so generic it told us nothing. We had 30 days to appeal, but the process ended with a canned rejection.

Your appeal may succeed, but your business must operate while you wait. Preparing in advance lets you keep going, whatever the outcome.

Our experience was grueling, but fortunately, two years earlier we had decoupled from the App Store by building a web version and making it our primary payment channel.

It also let us ship updates 10 times a day while escaping Apple’s predatory commissions. We weren’t the only ones. Pavel Durov, founder of Telegram, has also promoted web access to bypass store restrictions and potential censorship.

The lesson is straightforward. Customers need a working alternative before access disappears. Building one only after removal leaves the business exposed while the team races to replace its storefront.

We initially feared the user experience would suffer, but that concern proved unfounded. After the removal, every key metric fully recovered.

If you share this concern, test it while your app is still available to see whether customers can use and pay for the web version before they must rely on it.

Most founders see the App Store as a distribution channel, but rarely account for how much control it gives Apple over their business.

Before investing more in growth, examine how much revenue depends on continued access and what would survive a removal. Know how long the company could survive an unanswered appeal.

Investors should ask those questions too, because a growing subscription base deserves closer scrutiny when a single platform decision can interrupt its revenue. That exposure belongs in funding and valuation discussions.

Monopolies act in their interests, and if your business falls outside their vision, you may have little say in a decision that could destroy it.

You cannot control it, but you can decide whether it has the power to end your company. By building an alternative while your app is still available, you’ve made the wisest choice.

Yakov Filippenko is a seasoned entrepreneur with more than 10 years of experience in IT and technologies, as well as scaling businesses internationally. As a product manager at Yandex, he led a team that grew the product’s user base from 500,000 to 1.2 million and secured its entry into the international market. Subsequently, he co-founded SailPlay, which he scaled to 45 countries and eventually exited, after it was acquired by Retail Rocket in 2018. In 2021, Filippenko launched Intch, an AI-powered platform connecting part-time professionals with flexible roles.

#5357. ADA, XRP, DOGE: Gemini Names Biggest Losers of 2026

Crypto exchange Gemini has unveiled the biggest losers in the altcoin space for 2026 so far, as many of the crypto world's biggest digital currencies have been seeing massive double-digit price plunges.

Crypto exchange Gemini recently shared a list of 10 cryptocurrencies that have seen particularly brutal losses since the start of 2026 in a post on the X social media platform.

Topping Gemini's list of the biggest losers for this year is Bitcoin Cash (BCH), which has crashed a shocking 61.76% year-to-date.

Coming in second is Polkadot (DOT), with a 53.03% price decline, while Cardano (ADA) holds third place after shedding 48.04% of its value.

Ripple-related XRP and the top meme cryptocurrency Dogecoin (DOGE) are next in line, with losses of 43.43% and 42.38%, respectively.

Several other major cryptocurrencies are also seeing considerable losses, such as Sui (SUI), which has fallen 42.08%, Hedera (HBAR), which has dropped 38.13%, Solana (SOL), down 34.02%, Avalanche (AVAX), which has lost 33.40%, and Kaspa (KAS), which has gone down 30.75%.

Declining liquidity in the market, weakening speculative interest, lackluster institutional interest and general macroeconomic conditions are all major factors causing most major altcoins to underperform so far.

But for some, other issues within their ecosystems are also proving troublesome.

For instance, in the case of Cardano, the platform is seeing limited decentralized finance activity. As of Nov. 9, the total value locked in its DeFi ecosystem reportedly dropped below $50 million.

While Ripple continues its expansion in the institutional payments sector, stablecoin and tokenization areas, this hasn't necessarily led to sustained buying interest in XRP.

In fact, spot trading volume for XRP fell 53.5%, while perpetual futures trading volume dropped 44%.

Dogecoin, on the other hand, has been contending with waning speculative interest in meme cryptocurrencies.

Its institutional investment narrative also hasn't really caught on yet, with Bitwise announcing in September the shutdown of its Dogecoin ETF as the product failed to draw investor interest.

Bitcoin Cash has been seeing particularly sharp declines as it is now experiencing a reversal of its stellar 2025 performance, when the cryptocurrency soared around 38%.

Selling pressure picked up in May and June 2026 as BCH saw back-to-back monthly drops of over 30%.

A rebound could be seen in September after CME Group announced Bitcoin Cash futures, but this proved insufficient to stop the ongoing downtrend.

#5356. Bitcoin Price Rebounds Despite Quantum Threat as Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Faces Ouster After Two Affairs

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price has rebounded from recent lows as Nvidia board considers ousting CEO Jensen Huang following revelations about two extramarital affairs. Meanwhile, Glassnode data shows that 7.12 million BTC, worth more than $500 billion, already has publicly visible keys that future quantum computers could potentially exploit.

The developments put two of the technology industry’s biggest names under pressure. Bitcoin faces growing questions about its long-term cryptographic security, while Nvidia confronts a leadership crisis that could draw its AI dominance and ambitions in quantum computing.

Nvidia shares plunged more than 8% in extended trading after reports emerged that directors were preparing to remove Huang. The board is also considering an interim CEO before launching a wider search for a permanent replacement.

Bitcoin price recovered from its November 10 low of $72,600, reaching around $74,000 before easing to $73,700 this morning. The rebound offers bulls some relief after a sharp correction earlier this month. However, Glassnode has identified a potentially huge vulnerability affecting more than a third of Bitcoin’s issued supply.

According to a Glassnode update, approximately 35.4% of Bitcoin’s supply, equivalent to 7.12 million BTC, has publicly visible keys. At current market prices, those holdings are valued at more than $500 billion.

The exposure largely comes from address reuse. When Bitcoin holders spend from an address, their public keys become visible on the blockchain. Any remaining coins associated with those keys could become targets for sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Glassnode also says moving those coins to fresh addresses ends this exposure.

The concern centers on Shor’s algorithm, which could theoretically allow quantum computers to derive private keys from publicly available information. That would undermine the cryptographic security protecting vulnerable Bitcoin holdings.

Bitcoin developers are already exploring ways to address the challenge. BIP 360 proposes new transaction structures designed to reduce public-key exposure, while BIP 361 outlines a potential migration away from vulnerable signature schemes.

Nvidia’s leadership crisis has escalated dramatically after Reuters reported that its board was meeting late Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang. The 63-year-old founder has led Nvidia for more than three decades, transforming it into the dominant supplier of AI processors. But revelations about two extramarital relationships have triggered an internal investigation and intensified scrutiny of his leadership.

The first controversy involves Alice Huang, a businesswoman whose relationship with Jensen Huang has attracted attention from US intelligence officials. She is reportedly suspected of facilitating Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies. The investigation has raised concerns about potential Chinese intelligence involvement and whether Nvidia’s technology reached restricted customers.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, is now working with an "outside firm" to find a new CEO to replace Jensen Huang, per Bloomberg.The company is also reportedly weighing naming a temporary CEO while searching for a replacement.

A second relationship emerged through a New York Times report identifying Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Powell reportedly worked directly under Huang, creating additional corporate governance questions.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees, taking responsibility for his actions. The board’s response has shifted rapidly. Directors previously expressed confidence in Huang, but Bloomberg subsequently reported that Nvidia had engaged an outside firm to identify potential replacements.

It should be noted that Nvidia has 11 directors, with all but Huang considered independent. Its bylaws allow a majority vote to remove the CEO.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has emerged as a potential interim successor, while data-center executive Ian Buck has attracted attention as a possible longer-term candidate. The timing is particularly sensitive, with Nvidia scheduled to release quarterly results on November 17.

Bitcoin’s market recovery remains an important counterpoint for all these developments. Bitcoin price has managed to recover from its November 10 sell-off, with buyers stepping in around $72,700. Reclaiming $74,000 would give bulls another opportunity to challenge higher resistance levels.

The quantum threat is pushing developers to consider changes that could strengthen Bitcoin’s security over the coming years. Nvidia faces a different challenge. Losing Huang would remove the founder most closely associated with its AI dominance, potentially forcing investors to reassess the company’s leadership and long-term strategy.

The $500 billion quantum exposure has added another major scare to the market. But Bitcoin’s ability to adapt could become just as important as its price performance.

#5355. Protein Startups Are Selling Lots Of Snacks And Drinks. Our Sample Tasting Found Most Neither Great Nor Horrible

In a perfect world, we would all eat meals and snacks that are convenient, taste great and provide optimal nutrition.

In reality, however, there are tradeoffs. We crave ice cream, chips and candy bars, which make carbs and fat easy to over-consume. Meeting protein goals, meanwhile, can require conscientious effort, particularly for those, like your author, who aren’t keen on eating lots of meat.

Fortunately, as we chronicled earlier this week, both startups and established food brands are making it simpler than ever to up protein intake. From sodas to snack bars to ice cream, it’s now possible to get a fix of this coveted macronutrient with foods and drinks more commonly associated with sugar, starch and fat.

The looming question is: Do they taste good? To find out, we hit up a local Target for a selection of protein foods sold by venture-backed startups. I and a 10-year-old then subjected them to a taste test.

The verdict? Most of this stuff is indeed edible and drinkable, albeit almost never nearly as tasty as the more protein-deficient alternatives, with just one exception.

No. 1: David Vanilla Bean Frozen Dessert: Anyone who buys or consumes this particular ice cream alternative will be doing so for the nutritional content, not the taste. A single pint packs in a whopping 30 grams of protein and has just 210 calories. The texture is also on point, creamy and easy to spoon, with a distinct vanilla flavor.

That said, you can’t hide the fact that this is not a product made with your typical ice cream ingredients. Those who don’t like artificial sweeteners or the flavor and texture of whey protein will want to pass. For myself and my co-taster, however, it was a reasonably appealing eating experience. Not as good as traditional ice cream, but not bad for a high-protein food.

Made by: Medici Brands (David parent company).

No. 2 SkyPop Protein Soda: The nutritional stats for SkyPop Protein Soda are also remarkable. A 12-ounce can has just 45 calories, with 10 grams of protein and a single gram of carbohydrates. It’s also properly fizzy, and makes a satisfying pop when you open the can.

But what about flavor? Our local store only had the Ice Pop flavor in stock and it was, in both tasters’ view, not horrible but not something we’d plan to buy regularly. I could see consuming it when on a clear fluids diet, as is the case before some medical procedures, as it’d be one of the few available sources of protein.

No. 3: Khloud Protein Popcorn: Unlike many of our other featured foods, Khloud Protein Popcorn isn’t a super protein-rich offering. A serving contains 7 grams of protein and 160 calories, most of which come from carbs and fat. Still, its protein count is higher than other packaged popcorn, which typically has maybe 2 protein grams in a comparable serving.

Overall, the tasters’ conclusion, from our trial of White Cheddar Khloud, was that this is a decent snack food. The flavor of milk protein and whey protein concentrate was palpable, but not overwhelming. It’s not exactly a snack food to savor, but for something to casually munch at one’s desk or while watching a show, it served its purpose.

No. 4 Mosh: In the third season of “The White Lotus”, Mosh co-founder Patrick Schwarzenegger plays a fitness and finance bro who makes a daily high-protein shake that other family members find revolting. Perhaps this was inspired by Mosh, the brain-supporting protein bar startup he launched with his mother, Maria Shriver.

The Mosh bar, which we purchased in the peanut butter cup flavor, crams 20 grams of protein, 6 grams of fiber, plus brain-supporting ingredients like creatine and lion’s mane, into a compact, shelf-stable bar. It’s an impressive feat. Yet while our brains’ may have appreciated the nutrition and supplement boost the Mosh bar provided, our taste buds decidedly did not.

I’d put Mosh in the functional food category. It’s something that you might eat if you wanted that particular nutrient mix. But it’s not something to consume for pleasure.

No. 5 Cadootz Crackers: We tried two varieties of Cadootz Crackers — cheddar and sea salt — and walked away neither enthused nor repulsed.

For people interested in a gluten- and seed oil-free small snack cracker with about 5 grams of protein per serving, Cadootz rises to the occasion. It’s got a nice crunch and decent flavor.

As someone who’s not particularly seeking to avoid gluten and seed oils or to get a modest protein bump from my crackers, I’ll probably pass on follow-on purchases. But for its target audience, Cadootz should serve well.

No. 6 Frozen One: For those who thought the David frozen dessert was a marvel of protein engineering, the folks at Frozen One would like a word. Their protein ice cream has a whopping 40 grams of protein in each pint.

Yes, but how does it taste? Not that bad, according to our two-person tasting team. We tried both the chocolate and apple pie varieties, preferring the former. Like the David offering, Frozen One tastes like a product made with milk protein concentrate and sugar substitutes. You won’t mistake it for Ben and Jerry’s. But if the goal is to consume a steak-like quantity of protein in the form factor of a pint of ice cream, it does its job.

No. 7 Brami Protein Pasta: We saved the best for last. That, unexpectedly, was Brami Protein Pasta, a noodle made from semolina and lupini beans that boasts about 70% more protein than standard pasta and more than double the fiber.

With about 12 grams of protein for a 200 calorie serving, Brami isn’t a dense protein source. But, with the right topping, it’s enough to transform a typically starchy noodle meal into something reasonably protein rich.

Most notably, however, Brami tastes quite good, with no discernable weird aftertaste or texture issues. I made both standard and Brami noodles to taste the difference. For seconds, I went with the Brami.

#5354. Rothschild Investment Reveals XRP ETF Stake

Rothschild Investment LLC, the Chicago-based investment management firm, has filed its latest 13F with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), revealing its stake in the Bitwise XRP ETF.

Rothschild Investment’s filing, made on Nov. 10, indicates that the company has invested in 6,300 shares of the Bitwise XRP ETF.

Based on the information provided, these shares were worth $104,769 as of Sept. 30.

The investment in the Bitwise XRP ETF is listed under CUSIP 09174F107 in Rothschild Investment’s third-quarter report.

Interestingly, Rothschild Investment did not have any reported holdings of the XRP ETF in its previous quarterly filing, which indicates that the firm’s investment in the XRP ETF occurred in the third quarter of 2026.

The Bitwise XRP ETF, listed under the ticker XRP, was introduced in November 2025.

The ETF enables traditional investors to invest in the Ripple-linked cryptocurrency without needing to buy and hold XRP tokens themselves.

Although Rothschild Investment has invested in the XRP ETF, it is not a significant part of its overall portfolio.

The firm’s total portfolio value for 13F-reportable holdings is around $2.69 billion.

Rothschild Investment holds much larger stakes in Bitcoin and Ethereum investments.

When it comes to cryptocurrencies, Rothschild Investment’s largest holding is in the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF by BlackRock, where the company owns 40,188 shares worth around $1.9 million.

Additionally, Rothschild Investment reported holding $911,300 in the Grayscale Bitcoin Trust ETF and $335,160 in the Morgan Stanley Bitcoin Trust ETF.

Other Bitcoin-related investments include the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ETF ($125,113), VanEck Bitcoin ETF ($118,100), Bitwise Bitcoin ETF ($116,802) and Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ($2,107).

In total, the seven Bitcoin investments represent around $3.51 million in reported holdings.

Rothschild Investment also has stakes in the Grayscale Ethereum Staking ETF worth $538,622 and the Bitwise Ethereum ETF worth $476,500.

The company also has a significant holding in the Bitwise Crypto Industry Innovators ETF, with 24,250 shares worth $615,223.

The firm owns $38,360 worth of shares in the Grayscale CoinDesk Crypto 5 ETF.

Finally, it has invested $69,900 in a Solana ETF.

Aside from cryptocurrency investment funds, Rothschild Investment has shares in publicly traded companies that are heavily involved in the digital asset space.

Michael Saylor’s Strategy is one such holding, with a $530,763 investment.

Other holdings include Coinbase Global ($86,681), Block ($125,060) and Riot Platforms ($42,980), a Bitcoin mining company.

The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) has picked Avalanche as the only blockchain to settle tokenized stocks on its planned 24/7 trading platform, The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.

Tokenized stocks are blockchain tokens that track shares of real companies. The NYSE version would let investors trade U.S. stocks around the clock, settle trades instantly and pay with stablecoins, digital tokens that hold a steady $1 value.

The New York Stock Exchange has selected Avalanche ($AVAX) as the exclusive blockchain for settling tokenized U.S. stocks on its upcoming 24/7 trading platform, according to the WSJ.NYSE cited Avalanche’s speed, throughput and compliance capabilities.The platform is targeting… pic.twitter.com/uE4S3X5lnn

AVAX jumped on the news. It rose 4.3% in the minute the reports hit at 12:30 UTC, and it trades at $8.79 on Binance, up 11% on the day while Bitcoin and Ether are down.

The pick lands on a chain that holds only a small slice of the market today. Avalanche carries $179 million of the $3.73 billion in tokenized shares tracked by rwa.xyz. That is 4.8% of the market, down from 10.3% a month ago.

So can the NYSE deal make Avalanche the main home for these tokens?

The plan is not new, but the blockchain is. NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) first announced the platform in January and said it would seek regulatory approval.

The tokens would not be copies. ICE said they would be interchangeable with ordinary shares and carry the same dividend and voting rights.

NYSE picked Avalanche for its speed, the number of trades it can handle, and its tools for meeting regulatory rules, the Journal reported. The platform is aiming for a fourth-quarter launch, but it still needs regulators’ approval.

ICE has also signed up Securitize to issue tokenized shares for companies and funds, under a deal announced this year.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

The NYSE deal would be a big step up. We pulled the latest network breakdown from rwa.xyz, which tracks tokenized shares that investors can hold in their own wallets.

The market itself is still small next to the stock market. All the tokens it tracks add up to $3.73 billion, held by about 4.8 million wallet addresses.

The NYSE could change that scale. Every share settled through its platform would move on Avalanche, which no other chain can claim today.

There is a catch. Companies can refuse to have their shares tokenized. On OKXICE, a separate venue from OKX and ICE, 33 of the 62 companies first named had objected by late October.

Not yet. AVAX trades at $8.79 on Binance, up 11% from Monday’s opening price of $7.94, its best day since September 20.

The buying was heavy. In the hour that started at 12:00 UTC, about $11.8 million of AVAX changed hands on Binance. That is about 16 times a typical hour and the third-busiest hour in the past 1,000.

On the daily chart, AVAX is just below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that weight recent prices more. The 50-day and 200-day EMAs both sit at about $9.05, so one level now does the work of two.

#5352. Is the Crypto Market Walking Into a Bull Trap? Bitcoin ETF Records Five Straight Days of Outflow

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin’s latest recovery attempt is running into a serious problem: institutional investors are pulling money out of the market. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF recorded five consecutive days of net outflows, shedding $1.44 billion between November 5 and November 11.

Bitcoin is now trading near $73,500, struggling to reclaim the $75,000 level. Bitcoin ETF outflow streak raises a bigger question: Is the crypto market walking into another bull trap?

The timing is particularly concerning. Bitcoin briefly reclaimed $80,000 on November 4 before reversing sharply the following day. Crypto has since struggled to regain momentum, leaving us questioning buyers’ decisions and whether we are stepping in too early.

The latest Bitcoin ETF withdrawals included $430.2 million on November 5, followed by another $411.9 million on November 6. Outflows continued on November 9, 10, and 11.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for most of the selling pressure. The fund alone recorded $269.7 million in net outflows yesterday.

The latest Bitcoin ETF outflow streak shows that institutional demand is struggling to support the market’s recovery. Five consecutive sessions of withdrawals have removed $1.44 billion from U.S. spot Bitcoin funds. BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for three-quarters of that amount.

However, institutional demand has not disappeared entirely. Morgan Stanley’s Bitcoin ETF attracted $9 million yesterday, offering a small counterpoint to the ETF-wide selling.

Glassnode’s latest Week 46 report adds another warning. Bitcoin has fallen below the short-term holder cost basis of $75,600. This leaves recent buyers sitting on unrealized losses.

The research firm also points to shrinking stablecoin supply and continued ETF selling. Both developments display that fresh capital is struggling to enter the market.

This creates an uncomfortable setup for anyone buying the latest dip. A short-lived recovery could attract retail investors before another wave of selling pushes prices lower.

Bitcoin’s derivatives market offers another piece of the puzzle. BTC futures open interest remains above $50 billion, while funding rates remain positive. This number somehow paints a clear picture: leveraged traders are still paying to maintain bullish positions.

However, leverage has already started coming out of the market. Open interest has declined, and much of the long-side leverage near current prices has been flushed.

That creates two possible outcomes. If spot demand returns, reduced leverage could help Bitcoin recover without triggering another major liquidation cascade. Alternatively, another failed breakout could leave remaining leveraged buyers exposed to further downside.

For now, $75,600 is the important recovery threshold. Reclaiming that level would put Bitcoin back above the short-term holder cost basis and improve market sentiment.

A grinding climb toward $80,000 would offer stronger evidence that buyers are regaining control, but losing the $72,000 area could expose BTC to another test of $70,000.

The bull trap argument also has a counterpoint. There is accumulation among two large wallet cohorts, while selling momentum has started weakening. This shows that some investors are already positioning for a recovery.

The market does not need another dramatic crash to trap investors. Sometimes, all it takes is a convincing bounce that runs out of buyers.

#5351. webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

The card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It says TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight users want to hear.

On MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It says TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

Here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

None of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card shows the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a big generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 new tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

The card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

The useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

Chainlink sees a death cross approaching on the chart, with a solid possibility of an aggravation of the current state of affairs on the market. LINK is trading at around $10.49 at the moment, moving below every moving average on the daily chart.

The asset has already lost roughly a third of its value since the late September peak near $15.70, when the rally essentially ran out of steam.

The 50 EMA is rapidly diving down and most likely to cross the 100 EMA sooner rather than later. The 50 EMA sits near $11.70 right now, while the 100 EMA is around $11.40, so the gap between them is getting thin.

Luckily, volume is descending, so there's a good chance that things will stabilize rather than degrade from here. Daily volume in November is visibly lower than during the sell-off at the end of October, which is a good sign.

The lack of catalyst is the larger problem: ADA has no traction around it and there's certainly a chance that it won't appear in the foreseeable future.

#5349. The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Agentic AI And Infrastructure Are Still On A Roll

Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.

It was another big week for AI-related startup financings. Mirendil, a developer of agentic AI for R&D, led the pack with a $1 billion series A, followed by Mercor, which secured $750 million to connect AI developers with human experts.

Overall, the vast majority of this week’s largest rounds were AI-related, though we did see some biotech, fintech and enterprise software in the mix.

1. Mirendil, $1B, AI for R&D: Mirendil, a developer of agentic AI technology for research and development, secured $1 billion in a Series A funding. Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital led the round for the San Francisco-based startup.

2. Mercor, $750M, human-led AI training: Mercor, a platform that connects AI developers with human experts for model training and evaluation, raised $750 million in Series D funding. The round, backed by a long list of venture investors, set a $20 billion valuation for the San Francisco-based company, which was founded less than four years ago.

3. Torus, $500M, AI infrastructure: Salt Lake City-based Torus, a manufacturer of distributed power and compute infrastructure, announced a $500 million growth financing led by Magnetar Capital. It also introduced a product called Foundry, described as modular AI infrastructure for inference compute.

4. (tied) Path Robotics, $300M, AI for manufacturing: Path Robotics, a developer of physical AI technology for robotics and manufacturing, with initial expertise in welding, picked up $300 million in Series E financing. Georgian led the round, which set a $2.45 billion valuation for the Columbus, Ohio-based company.

4. (tied) LangChain, $300M, agentic AI: LangChain, developer of a platform to run, improve and govern AI agents, closed on $300 million in Series C funding at a $3 billion valuation. CapitalG led the round for the 4-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

6. Nominal, $240M, hardware engineering tools: Nominal, a developer of intelligence tools for hardware engineering, raised $240 million at a $3 billion valuation. Lightspeed Venture Partners and Insight Partners led the round for the Austin-based startup.

7. (tied) Imprint, $130M, fintech: Imprint, a payments, loyalty and customer intelligence platform for brands, landed $130 million in new funding at a $1.9 billion valuation. Khosla Ventures led the financing for the 6-year-old, New York-based company.

7. (tied) Mavria, $130M, AI infrastructure: Mavria, a startup focused on standardizing how AI infrastructure is developed, built and deployed, launched publicly and said it has raised $130 million in pre-seed and seed funding to date. Its latest round, led by Paradigm, sets a $1 billion valuation for the startup, whose founders formerly worked at the U.S. Department of Energy.

9. (tied) Delix Therapeutics, $100M, biotech: Delix Therapeutics, a startup that says it has “reverse-engineered and optimized psychedelics” to develop treatments for psychiatric and psychological disorders, closed on $100 million in Series C funding. Johnson & Johnson Innovation and SV Health Investors’ Dementia Discovery Fund led the financing for the Bedford, Massachusetts-based company.

9. (tied) Rox, $100M, sales automation: San Francisco-based Rox, developer of an AI revenue agent for enterprise sales, announced a $100 million Series B financing led by General Catalyst and March Capital.

9. (tied) Databento, $100M, financial market data: Databento, a finance data platform, secured $100 million in Series C funding at a $1.1 billion valuation. Fifth Down Capital led the round for the Salt Lake City-based company.

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Nov. 7-13, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

#5348. Ripple's David Schwartz Reveals Massive XRP Sale

The XRP holdings of former Ripple CTO David Schwartz have plummeted by a massive 23M XRP. David Schwartz, former chief technology officer of Ripple, has disclosed that he has sold the overwhelming majority of his XRP holdings over time.

As a result, his crypto holdings have taken a massive hit. Taking to the social media platform X recently, Schwartz shared that he has gone from holding around 26M XRP at one point to just 3M XRP.

That's a massive reduction of around 23M XRP. This represents a decrease of over 88% from his peak XRP holdings.

"It's not a secret. I think I'm down from a high of around 26 million XRP to around 3 million XRP," David Schwartz divulged.

Schwartz has also revealed that he has slashed his Bitcoin holdings from around 1,500 BTC all the way down to just 1 BTC. He has gone even further with his Ethereum holdings too (from around 40,000 ETH to just 6 ETH).

As such, Schwartz has sold off nearly all his previous Bitcoin and Ethereum holdings.

It is not clear when he made the bulk of his sales or how much he made from them.

Schwartz's latest update comes after a few different revelations about his crypto sales tactics.

As reported by U.Today, the former Ripple CTO recently admitted to selling around 2.5M XRP in 2025 alone.

Most of these tokens were received in 2020 and 2023, according to Schwartz.

He revealed that he had to pay around $1.7 million in capital gains taxes on his sales.

The Ripple veteran has repeatedly justified his crypto sales by citing his extremely low risk tolerance.

In July, Schwartz even disclosed that he and his wife had decided to sell off some of their crypto holdings whenever new all-time highs were reached.

Most recently, he detailed that he has a written sales plan set up with a lawyer at least 30 days before selling his XRP.

He has admitted that he hasn't been buying XRP for a long time now.

At the same time, Schwartz does still hold a significant amount of Ripple stock, but that also leaves him exposed to more financial risk than he'd ideally prefer.

The revelation comes at a time when there is mounting frustration among the XRP community over the cryptocurrency's lackluster price performance.

At the start of this month, Schwartz was called out by an XRP holder wondering if he was somehow to blame for the token's downturn.

As reported by U.Today, the former Ripple CTO stressed that he probably had very little impact.

#5345. Crunchbase Data: Nvidia’s Startup Funding Deals Hit A Record. What’s Next After Huang?

Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026.

The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data, already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-company investor.

With co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China, we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold.

Nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall.

Nvidia’s startup investments this year total 121 and span AI model developers, data center operators, robotics startups and healthcare companies. That continues the broad approach we examined last year, when the company and its venture arm participated in 91 known startup financings, up from 54 the year prior.

The largest Nvidia-backed deals in 2026 include OpenAI’s Series G, which closed at $122 billion in March, and Anthropic’s $30 billion Series G in February. (Those figures represent the entire rounds, including other investors’ contributions, rather than Nvidia’s individual checks.)

The company also participated in a $3.9 billion September Series F for AI infrastructure provider Crusoe and a roughly $3.5 billion September Series D for model developer Mistral AI.

Of course, large as those deals are, Nvidia’s startup bets represent a small fraction of the company’s incredible market capitalization. Even as its share price tumbled this week with Huang’s departure and the surrounding news, Nvidia’s valuation remains close to $4 trillion.

NVentures’ activity shows how far that investment footprint extends beyond the best-known model developers.

The venture arm’s larger bets this year include robot intelligence developer Skild AI’s $1.4 billion January Series C, and autonomous driving startup Waabi’s $750 million Series C in the same month. It also backed two rounds for Bedrock Robotics, which develops technology to automate construction equipment: a $270 million Series B in February and a $600 million Series C in October. Its healthcare investments included a $150 million April Series E for medical imaging AI company Aidoc.

As in years past, Nvidia and NVentures usually participate alongside other investors. The company or its venture arm are listed as lead or co-lead investors in about 1 in 5 of its deals this year, per Crunchbase data.

For startups, Nvidia’s value as an investor also extends beyond its deep pockets. NVentures describes its offering as access to technical teams, technology integrations and help reaching customers.

Nvidia’s new leadership could bring a different approach to risk. Before this week’s news, CFO and now interim CEO Collette Kress had pushed back on Huang’s increasingly large AI investments, Reuters reported this week, citing two people familiar with the matter.

Nvidia’s board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption. That assurance leaves the pace of future investments an open question. With earnings scheduled for Nov. 17, founders and investors will be watching for signs of how much of Huang’s investment playbook continues under new leadership.

As of Tuesday, November 10, the Bitcoin vs gold race has an unusual score for 2026: both are losing. Bitcoin (BTC) is down 15.1% this year, and gold is down 5.9%.

That is rare. We compared the two assets’ returns up to November 10 in every year since 2015. Both were down at this point only twice before, in 2018 and 2022.

Gold is still ahead on the year. Gold futures trade at $4,086 an ounce, 23% below their record close of $5,318 on January 29. Bitcoin, at $74,259, is 40.5% below its record close of $124,753 from October 2025.

The calendar favors gold too. In each of the past 11 years, whichever asset led on November 10 also finished the year ahead.

But 2018 and 2022 ended the same way: Bitcoin hit its cycle low within six weeks and then beat gold by a wide margin the next year. So is 2026 setting up the same turn for 2027?

The two earlier cases point the same way, though two cases are a small sample to build on.

Both rebounds came in the year before a Bitcoin halving, the event every four years that cuts the number of new coins miners receive by half. The halvings fell in 2020 and 2024, and the next one is expected in 2028. That puts 2027 in the same slot as 2019 and 2023.

This year itself looks settled. Bitcoin beat gold in 8 of the 11 full years since 2015, and gold won only in 2018, 2022 and 2025. In every one of those 11 years, the asset that led on November 10 stayed ahead to December 31. Gold leads by about nine percentage points, so history hands it 2026, its second win in a row.

Gold’s slide has been steep for a metal. It closed at a record $5,318 on January 29, fell as low as $3,899 on October 30, and now trades at $4,086.

Investors have not walked away. Gold exchange-traded funds (ETFs) hold physical gold and trade like stocks. Worldwide, they added $2.7 billion in October, their fourth straight month of inflows, the World Gold Council reported on November 5. Their holdings rose 19 tonnes to a record 4,275 tonnes. Over the first ten months of the year, the funds took in $41 billion, the third-strongest run on record. North American funds were the exception, with small outflows.

Bitcoin has done better since February. Measured in gold, one Bitcoin bought 21.1 ounces on January 5. By February 23, that had fallen to 12.4 ounces, the lowest since March 2023. It now buys 18.2 ounces.

The gap since that February low is wide. Bitcoin is up 14.9% since February 23, while gold is down 21.8%. Since June 30, Bitcoin has gained 26.8% and gold 1.2%.

#5339. Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

According to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

Those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

Denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

The sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

Timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

This removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

App developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

This is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams plan to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

The coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

#5338. Deutsche Bank Opens Digital Asset Custody to Paying Institutional Clients

Deutsche Bank opens up digital asset custody to paying institutional clients. The service includes storage, user experience improvements, and accessibility via the bank's own gateways. The bank announced the launch on November 11, as DB's official website reveals.

This is an improvement in the field of institutional adoption, even though it comes at a time when it might be unwarranted. The market is experiencing serious issues and constant outflows from both retail and institutional investors.

Surprisingly, the bank can provide both warm and cold storage options available directly through DB's infrastructure. According to the landing page, the platform will provide key storage via Hardware Security Modules. Access goes through Autobahn, the bank's own multi-channel gateway.

Compliance will also be handled by Deutsche Bank. Initially, the service will focus on core functions: custody of digital assets and transfers, with further capabilities planned.

The Asian market has yet to receive similar treatment. For now, the service is available in the EU, operating out of DB AG Frankfurt. An expansion to Asia is reportedly planned for 2027, though the details are yet to be confirmed.

Additionally, DB announced support for euro stablecoins such as EURC and EURAU, in addition to BTC, ETH, and USDC. This is an attempt to promote the adoption of EU-issued stablecoins as part of a strategy aimed at moving away from USDT dominance. EURAU is issued by AllUnity, a joint venture that includes DWS, the asset manager majority-owned by Deutsche Bank.

Self-custody or banks: that is the real question here. Industry experts such as Bloomberg's ETF analyst Eric Balchunas suggest that self-custody has been a worse option and that a custodian with funds protection and insurance is a better option for regular investors. Even Binance founder CZ admitted after the Ledger incident that self-custody comes with extra responsibilities.

Back in August, a Coldcard exploit drained 1,816 BTC from more than 5,000 cold-storage addresses, according to Fortune.

However, it puts some pressure on those who might receive their funds from grey sources. Unfortunately for them, a bank custodian creates another barrier, as every deposit has to go through the bank's compliance checks.

NVIDIA tokenized stocks traded through a shock on Sunday, November 8, when news about Nvidia’s CEO broke while Wall Street was closed. At 20:12 UTC, CNBC reported that Nvidia’s board was investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China.

The stock market was closed. Tokenized versions of Nvidia, which trade around the clock on crypto platforms, were not. Within 30 minutes, Nvidia’s market on Hyperliquid fell 3.3%.

By the time Wall Street opened on Monday, 18 hours later, the token traders had already found the price. Hyperliquid’s Nvidia market stood at $173.27 a minute before the opening bell. Nvidia opened at $173.07, just 0.1% away.

Nvidia reports earnings on November 17, after the market closes. So can tokenized stocks call the move again?

The weekend gave tokenized markets a clean test. Nvidia closed Friday at $186.64 on the Nasdaq, and nothing traded on Wall Street until pre-market trading opened at 4 a.m. in New York on Monday, or 09:00 UTC.

We tracked Nvidia’s price on Hyperliquid minute by minute. The market there is a perpetual contract run by trade.xyz, a type of futures contract with no expiry date that follows the share price.

Backed tokens moved the same way. NVIDIA xStock (NVDAx), a token on Solana backed by real Nvidia shares, fell from $188.13 on Sunday at 20:00 UTC to $175.98 by 08:00 UTC on Monday. Hourly prices on CoinGecko show the same overnight slide.

Crypto Expert Report: What is the Best Meme Coin to Buy and Forget Until the Next Bullrun?

The news pulled in traders. Between Friday’s close and Monday’s pre-market, $258.5 million worth of Nvidia traded on Hyperliquid.

That is 4.7 times the average of the four weekends before, when the same 60-hour window saw $33 million to $72 million.

The timing explains it. Over a normal weekend, almost nothing happens to Nvidia, so the tokenized market is quiet. This weekend, it was one of the few places where traders could act on the news for about 13 hours.

There is an irony here. On November 2, Nvidia joined the companies objecting to tokenized versions of their shares on OKXICE, the planned venue from NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and the crypto exchange OKX.

The next big Nvidia news will also land when Wall Street is mostly closed. Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday, November 17, after the market closes, with a call at 5 p.m. in New York.

The regular after-hours session runs until 8 p.m. in New York. From then until 4 a.m., tokenized markets are among the few places still trading Nvidia.

The test will be harder this time. Weekend news hit a quiet market with one clear direction. Earnings bring a flood of numbers at once, and the first move after a report often reverses.

Nvidia trades at $173.17 on the Nasdaq on Tuesday, down 3.1% after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data. It touched $170.12, its lowest price since March 31. It is 28% below its record close of $239.24 on October 6.

On Hyperliquid’s four-hour chart, where each candle covers four hours, Nvidia sits below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that give recent prices more weight. The 50-period EMA stands at $189.53 and the 200-period EMA at $206.78.

#5330. Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path shows how far the probing went.

One token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

Loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, says user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

The loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction shows a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

An independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

The numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

That arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

The harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

That detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

Loopscale's November 6 update named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale says its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

So the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team says it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

Loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

The two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

The loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

The takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

Vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

This looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem shows pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

#5322. A YC startup is putting $1M behind 5 unsolved materials science problems for AI

Discovered Materials, a months-old San Francisco startup using AI models to find new substances for building advanced chips, announced a million-dollar challenge for AI models to solve five critical problems in materials science.

While frontier AI models have solved a remarkable series of outstanding mathematics problems and made progress in the life sciences, they have yet to truly plumb the complex physics in advanced materials.

“It’s more difficult to specify problems clearly in materials science because it’s not like math, where you have a very specific definition and can get to a yes or no,” said Advaith Sridhar, a co-founder of Discovered Materials, which was part of Y Combinator’s spring 2026 batch. “We came to this discussion [wondering], what are the grand challenges in this field? How do we know AI is making progress?”

Though materials science doesn’t have an equivalent of the Millennium Prize Problems, Discovered Materials recruited an advisory group of academics at leading global universities to spell out five open problems. The company is offering a pool of prizes, worth $1 million in total, for solutions to the problems.

“Across materials science, there are phenomena we observe but cannot explain,” Felipe Jornada, a Stanford professor who helped develop the challenges, said in a statement. “Explaining these phenomena would improve our understanding of physics, and the answers would directly shape how we build electronics, store energy, and manufacture the materials of the future.”

Before announcing the challenges, Discovered Materials turned frontier lab models loose on them, giving AI agents internet access and other resources to work autonomously for days. The models spent several days on each problem without making much headway. Still, it’s easy to imagine OpenAI or Anthropic attempting to one-shot them with significantly more compute or a newer model.

“It’s not particularly a concern to us whether we find it, or someone else finds it, or a professor finds it, or the frontier labs find it,” Sridhar said. “The reason we’re putting out these challenges is because we want them to serve as the goalposts. If you go and solve these challenges, we are deepening our understanding of materials and how things around us behave.”

Tracking efforts to solve the problems will show “whether the models are climbing in this domain,” he added.

The challenge also reflects the changing nature of scientific inquiry as AI proves capable of uncovering insights and techniques human researchers didn’t anticipate. With solutions apparently easier to find than ever, the questions become more important.

“This is a new way of thinking about science, where we come up with the verification and the challenges first, and then we let somebody come up with the ideas that explain the problem,” Sridhar said. “Knowing what are the right questions to ask is not trivial and very difficult in this domain, so this is where the professors have really helped us shape what are the right questions we should be asking.”

Discovered Materials’ main focus is developing new materials for use in semiconductors; the startup partners with chip giants on research projects while also funding its own scientific efforts. When the company announced its seed round in August, Sridhar told TechCrunch that he hoped the company would generate a useful material within a year.

“Those timelines have accelerated a little bit,” he says today. “I’m more confident now that we will be able to find these industrially useful materials in a timeline shorter than a year.”

Deutsche Bank opened its digital asset custody service to institutional and corporate clients on Wednesday, November 11, starting with Bitcoin, Ether and three stablecoins. Germany’s largest bank now holds the private keys to clients’ coins itself, three years after it first applied for a German crypto custody licence.

The launch lands in a gloomy market. Bitcoin trades at $73,943, down 5.8% in a week. That is 41% below its October 2025 record of $126,080.

The crowd is gloomier still. Analytics firm Santiment counts more negative than positive social media comments on BTC, Ether and XRP. It reads that disbelief as a sign of a classic bullish counter signal, the idea that markets tend to turn when most traders expect them to fall.

We checked that idea against eight years of the Crypto Fear & Greed Index. It works, but only at the extremes.

The service does two things at the start. It stores clients’ coins and moves them on request, between the bank’s own warm and cold wallets or out to third parties. Trading is not part of it.

The bank’s custody site lists the details:

Clients reach it through Autobahn, the same platform they already use for the bank’s other services. That is the selling point for a corporate treasurer: no new crypto firm to vet, and no in-house wallet team to build.

#5318. Aina’s smart ring has a screen, a joystick, and a mic so you can talk to AI agents

Hardware startup Aina released a smart ring today that features a screen, a joystick, and a mic so that you can talk to your agents and take notes. The $399 ring has a speaker so you can take calls using it as well.

The startup, which raised $5.5 million in July, is positioning the ring as a controller of sorts for both AI and non-AI apps.

The company previously made Mirage, a three-key controller that let you invoke buttons based on the app on your Mac’s screen. For instance, if you were on a Google Meet call, you could map keys to camera on/off, mic mute/unmute, or to leave the meeting.

Aina has baked in lessons from that device to create the new ring, which it’s simply calling “AI ring.” Using its mic, you can take notes, send a prompt to agents, set reminders, and dictate notes on your Mac using Wispr Flow or the startup’s own dictation engine.

Now, there are already smart rings in the market that do similar things, like the Pebble Index 01, Sandbar Stream, Oasis, and Natura, which is probably why Aina has added more controls and functionality to stand out. Its ring comes with a speaker so that you can take calls, and there is a screen, which lets you see notifications from your phone or which apps you are controlling.

For navigation, there is a joystick, and it also supports gestures, so that it can trigger different actions based on what’s on your Mac or phone’s screen. The ring also lets you control music or even smart home devices like Apple TV.

I have used the ring for a few days, and it feels like a smartwatch in a ring format, with more controls. I can get notifications and reply to them. It surfaces my meetings; I can call Uber if I want to get a ride home.

It’s easier to use Apple TV’s remote itself, but the Aina ring proved useful the couple times I couldn’t find the remote. Granted, a lot of the software and features are still being fleshed out, so it’s hard to figure out where such a device ring might sit in my daily usage, but it is squarely aimed at folks who are surrounded by digital devices and AI applications.

“Phones and laptop screens were designed for an age of browsing where you think about opening apps. For interacting with proactive agents, we need a better interface, and that is what we had in mind while designing Aina,” Apoorv Shankar, Aina’s founder, told TechCrunch over a call.

Companies are trying to cater to programmers and AI enthusiasts with specialized hardware that could help them harness different agents. This includes OpenAI’s experimental keyboard and Rabbit trying to position itself as a controller. The hope with such hardware is that enough people will have multiple agents running to invest in specific gadgets to keep tabs on them.

Aina’s ring goes on preorder starting Thursday at early-bird pricing of $399, and the company plans to start shipping the device in January 2027. Once the early-bird period ends, the ring will cost $499.
